definition: Syncretism means the blending of separate traditions into one.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word syncretism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know syncretism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Food writers call the delta city's signature stew a syncretism: three kitchens' techniques simmered into one dish no single tradition can claim.
Borrowing stops short of syncretism — one tradition lifts a single element, a word or a spice, and both go on being themselves, while a syncretism weaves whole traditions into one.
Absorption goes further than syncretism — a syncretism weaves traditions into a new shared one; absorption swallows one tradition into another until nothing of it stands apart.

Fusion is any melting-together at all — cuisines, genres, atomic nuclei — casual enough for a food-truck menu. Syncretism is the scholar's narrower term: specifically traditions or belief systems blending, over real history, into a genuinely new one whose seams no longer show.

A hybrid is the crossbred product — the offspring itself, the thing you can point to once the mixing is done. Syncretism names the blending instead: the long process by which separate traditions grow into one. The hybrid is the result; the syncretism is how it came to be.

Plutarch told of Crete's feuding cities closing ranks the moment an outsider attacked — synkretismos, 'joining together like the Cretans.' Whether or not his tale is the true origin, the mysterious middle of this word built nothing else in English. Remember the story instead: separate traditions banding together until they grow into one.
Syncretism means the blending of separate traditions into one.

The mill-town wedding rite is a syncretism grown from generations of mixed marriages: a canopy from one faith, a ribbon-binding from another, readings in two languages — and every family treats it as one ceremony, not a patchwork.
Syncretism is the anthropologist's word for traditions fusing into a genuinely new one — religions, musics, rituals.
Mere borrowing lifts an element and moves on; coexistence keeps the threads side by side.
In a true syncretism the threads stop being separable at all.
Syncretism is an academic term — religion, anthropology, music history — for traditions that have genuinely become one.

Anthropologist Marisol Vega spent a decade studying the winter festival of San Telmo, a mountain town on the old trade road between two empires.
Church records from the 1600s describe missionary priests staging saints' processions in the plaza.
Ledgers from the same century record payments to masked dancers whose steps came from valley harvest rites far older than the church.
For generations the two performances circled each other.
Then the masks entered the processions; the saints acquired the dancers' bells; the harvest songs took on Latin refrains.

What visitors see today, Vega argues, is a true syncretism: not one tradition decorated with another, but a third thing, grown over four centuries, that neither ancestor community would fully recognize.
When officials tried to separate the church elements from the valley elements for a heritage application, the town could not agree where one ended and the other began.
